briefing.hook: At 8:58 AM, Meridian Robotics lost control of its flagship factory for exactly seven minutes.
briefing.context: During the blackout, one automated production line produced 312 defective components, and an unreleased prototype vanished from a locked testing room.
briefing.tension: The access system records show that the testing room was never opened.
briefing.objective: Determine how the prototype disappeared, who sabotaged the production line, and whether the two incidents were connected.

truth.incident: The apparent factory blackout was deliberately triggered by Nadia Cross, the company's quality director, but she did not steal the prototype. She created the blackout to destroy a batch of defective components that would have exposed a manufacturing fraud. The prototype disappeared through an automated materials corridor rather than the locked testing room.
truth.whatHappened: Nadia deliberately caused a seven-minute systems outage and used the confusion to trigger an automated disposal cycle that removed the defective components. During the same outage, Leon Park, a junior automation engineer, used an unrelated maintenance override to move the prototype through a materials corridor because he intended to secretly copy its design for a rival startup. The two events overlapped accidentally.
truth.motive: Nadia wanted to destroy evidence of manufacturing irregularities that threatened her position. Leon wanted to steal technical information for personal financial gain.
truth.method: Nadia triggered the network outage through a maintenance subsystem. Leon used the same outage as cover to activate an automated materials-transfer route.
truth.centralTwist: There are two independent wrongdoings during the same seven-minute window.
truth.finalTruth: The sabotage and prototype theft were committed by different people for different reasons. The apparent single conspiracy is false.

timeline.description: All four characters arrive at Meridian Robotics.
Nadia reviews a quality-control report showing a suspicious spike in rejected components.
Leon requests access to the automation control room.
Maya notices several defective components have been quarantined.
Owen begins a scheduled inspection of the prototype testing room.
Leon opens an engineering workstation to prepare an unauthorized maintenance override.
Nadia accesses the factory maintenance subsystem.
The factory experiences a seven-minute systems outage.
Nadia triggers an automated disposal cycle that removes the quarantined defective batch.
Leon activates a materials-transfer route and moves the prototype out of the testing-room sector.
Maya sees a materials cart moving through a corridor but cannot see its contents.
Owen discovers the prototype is missing.
Quality-control staff discover that the defective batch is gone.
Management assumes the blackout was a coordinated theft and sabotage operation.

questions.text: What were you doing when the systems went down?

variants.text: I was in my office reviewing quality reports.
I was dealing with the morning quality reports.
I was where I needed to be. The important thing is the failure itself.
I was checking one of the automation workstations.
I was in the engineering bay.
The systems were failing everywhere. I was trying to understand why.
I was near the production floor.
I was checking the quarantined components.
I was checking the prototype room.

questions.text: Was the prototype room ever opened during the outage?

variants.text: No. The access system never recorded an opening.
Not through the normal entrance.

questions.text: Did you see anything unusual during the blackout?

variants.text: A materials cart moved through the corridor. That route shouldn't have been active.
I saw a cart moving toward the materials corridor.
I saw something moving. It looked like a cart.

questions.text: Were you concerned about the defective production batch?

variants.text: Everyone was concerned. It was becoming a serious operational problem.
Not particularly. Production problems happen.
I was focused on fixing the problem, not discussing it.

questions.text: Was the defective batch actually supposed to be destroyed?

variants.text: No. It was quarantined for review.
Not until management finished investigating the failures.

questions.text: Why did the materials-transfer system activate during the outage?

variants.text: That system has automated safeguards. It could have been a fault.
I don't know. I wasn't operating it.

questions.text: You told me you weren't operating the materials system. The override log shows an unauthorized engineering command.

variants.text: That log doesn't identify me.
I used the system. I did not take anything from the room.
Fine. I moved something. I never expected the outage to happen.

questions.text: Why were you interviewing with another company?

variants.text: I wasn't.
I wanted better opportunities.
They wanted to hire me. I thought the prototype would make me valuable.

questions.text: Could the prototype have left the room without the room door opening?

variants.text: Not through the room itself. But there are service routes connected to the materials system.

questions.text: Why was the quarantined batch destroyed during the outage?

variants.text: I didn't authorize any disposal.
The system may have interpreted the outage incorrectly.
The batch was becoming a liability.

questions.text: You said the outage was an accident. The maintenance records show your credentials triggered it.

variants.text: My credentials don't prove I was responsible.
I caused the outage. I did not steal the prototype.
Yes. I triggered it. I needed the defective batch gone before the report was reviewed.

questions.text: Why didn't you initially mention the materials cart?

variants.text: I wasn't sure it mattered.
I thought it might be unrelated.
There was a lot happening during those seven minutes.

questions.text: Did you copy the quality report before the incident?

variants.text: No.
I made a copy because I didn't trust management.
Yes. I was planning to protect the report from being altered.

questions.text: Nadia caused the outage, but that doesn't explain the prototype. What did you move through the materials corridor?

variants.text: Nothing that belonged to Meridian.
I moved equipment. I made a terrible decision.
The prototype. I took it because I thought I could sell the design.

contradictions.description: Owen establishes that the testing room never opened, conflicting with the assumption that someone stole the prototype directly from the room.
The materials-transfer system activated during the same outage in which the prototype disappeared.
Leon initially claims he was not operating the materials system, but the engineering override log shows unauthorized activity.
Nadia claims the outage was accidental, but maintenance records attribute the trigger to her credentials.
The same seven-minute window contains two independently motivated actions.

reveal.headline: There were two crimes hiding inside one blackout.
narrative: Nadia Cross deliberately triggered the factory outage because she needed the defective production batch destroyed before an executive review exposed how quality failures had been repeatedly reclassified.
She succeeded in destroying that evidence.
Leon Park noticed the outage and used the same window to activate the automated materials corridor.
He moved the prototype through the corridor, intending to copy or sell its design.
He did not know Nadia had planned the outage.
Nadia did not know Leon intended to steal the prototype.
The investigation initially assumes one coordinated conspiracy because two major incidents happened during the same seven minutes.
Owen's security records prove the prototype room itself was never opened.
Maya's observation of the materials cart establishes another route.
The maintenance override links that route to Leon.
The quality records and disposal event separately establish Nadia's motive and responsibility for the blackout.
The critical deduction is therefore not simply identifying a culprit. It is recognizing that the apparent single mystery is actually two overlapping acts committed independently.
